title: Homeland Security scales back plans for Williamsport detention center — for now
summary: The Department of Homeland Security said in court filings Thursday that it is initially planning to hold 542 immigrants in a Williamsport warehouse it hopes to convert to a detention center, not the 1,500 that might eventually be housed there.
content:
by Maryland Matters Staff, Maryland Matters April 6, 2026

by Maryland Matters Staff, Maryland Matters April 6, 2026

The Department of Homeland Security said in court filings Thursday that it is initially planning to hold 542 immigrants in a Williamsport warehouse it hopes to convert to a detention center, not the 1,500 that might eventually be housed there.

The filings, first reported Friday by the Baltimore Banner, were part of the department’s effort to block a preliminary injunction against work on the site sought by the state of Maryland, which has sued to stop the project.

The department said it has complied with all the environmental and other regulations for the lower number of detainees. Any work required on the facility for the initial number of detainees would be within the current footprint and would not disturb surrounding areas, the court filings said.

U.S. District Judge Brendan Hurson last month issued a two-week order halting construction on the site, then extended it through April 17, to give both sides a chance to argue for a more permanent injunction.

Hurson’s latest order stopped Immigration and Customs Enforcement from “proceeding with renovation and/or construction activities required to build, retrofit, or otherwise convert the Williamsport Warehouse … into an immigration detention facility.”

Maryland asked for the order, saying it feared ICE would rush to begin construction while the suit against the project was pending. It said that would have caused irreparable damage to the local environment and to water and sewer infrastructure.

In its request for an emergency injunction, the state said ICE has moved with “unrelenting speed” to convert the 825,000-square-foot warehouse into a processing and detention center capable of holding up to 1,500 immigrants, with little public notice and little input.

After buying the warehouse in January for $102 million, ICE quietly performed a historical review of the site and invited public input on the fact that the facility sits in a 100- to 500-year floodplain. But it has not held public hearings and has not met with local officials on the project.

ICE last month awarded a $113 million contract to KVG LLC of Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, “to immediately retrofit the warehouse into this massive immigration detention facility,” the state said in its petition. Hurson noted that the KVG contract was awarded the day after the public comment period closed on the floodzone, and it had a start date of March 6: “Presumably, then, the renovation has already begun.”

But DHS said the only work done so far has been planning, although security and repair work needs to be done. Any work done on the site now would be done within the confines of the warehouse itself — roof and HVAC repairs, for example — or would include such work as installation of security fencing and security cameras at the site.

It would not be the environmentally disruptive work described by the state, the department said. Maryland has not met “its burden to demonstrate that the facility will result in irreparable harm to its interests,” the filing said.

In his initial order, Hurson said an emergency injunction was merited because the state is likely to prevail on its claims that ICE failed to meet standards of the National Environmental Policy Act, which would require an environmental impact statement or an environmental assessment of the project, neither of which has been done.

Republicans applaud immigrant detention — until it’s in their back yards

“On the record before the Court at this time, the State has shown that Defendants likely failed to comply with their obligations under NEPA,” Hurson wrote. “Defendants do not appear to have taken a ‘hard look’ at the potential environmental consequences of their plans for the Williamsport Warehouse.”

Hurson also said the state would likely “suffer irreparable harm” if work was allowed to proceed before the state’s lawsuit can be heard.

But DHS said it has met all the NEPA requirements needed for the project as currently envisioned: For 542 detainees, including “448 typical dormitory pods, 32 disability
accessible dormitory pods, and 62 pods designated for behavioral and special housing needs.”

The facility “could ultimately house 1,500 detainees,” said a court statement from an official overseeing the project. “Once those plans are nearer finalization, ICE will conduct additional NEPA analysis based on those plans before it makes a final decision on its plan for retrofitting the warehouse for housing detainees.”

The state is scheduled to respond by Thursday to the DHS filing, and Hurson is supposed to issue a ruling by April 16.
